a: Treat matching the anchor to its positive as a classification problem over candidate positives and negatives. For a batch of N query–positive pairs, each query scores all N documents; off-diagonal documents act as negatives.
notation: s is a similarity score; τ > 0 is temperature. The denominator includes the positive. With multiple relevant documents, define a multi-positive loss or mask false negatives.
nuance: Lower temperature sharpens the distribution and emphasizes high-scoring mistakes; it is not unconditionally better. More batch candidates offer more discrimination but also more false negatives. Symmetric query→document and document→query losses are optional, task-dependent choices.
detail: Picture an `N × N` grid where row `i` is query `q_i` and column `j` is document `d_j`: InfoNCE is literally standard `N`-way softmax cross-entropy asking each row to pick its matching diagonal partner `d_i` out of `N − 1` batch distractors! Temperature `τ` controls how picky the softmax is: tiny `τ` zooms in fiercely on the single hardest distractor; huge `τ` treats all mistakes gently.
example: With batch size N=1,024, computing just 2,048 embeddings gives you 1,024 × 1,023 ≈ 1M negative comparisons for free via one matrix multiply `Q @ D.T`!
follow: Why can increasing batch size from 256 to 32,768 actually *hurt* retrieval if your corpus has many duplicate or equivalent documents?

q: Triplet loss versus contrastive softmax?
a: Triplet loss pushes one negative past one positive by a fixed margin `m`; contrastive softmax (InfoNCE) contrasts each positive against *all* `N−1` negatives in the batch at once. **In practice:** **in-batch InfoNCE** (paired with mined hard negatives, or **SigLIP** pairwise sigmoid) is the modern default for text, search and multimodal embeddings because easy triplets waste ~90% of compute at zero gradient; **triplet loss** is mostly legacy or niche fixed-threshold verification.
notation: \(m>0\) is a margin; \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) is the chosen distance. State whether it is Euclidean, squared Euclidean or another metric.
nuance: An easy triplet beyond the margin gives zero loss and gradient. Very hard negatives may be mislabeled positives. Contrastive training is not automatically superior if the supervision or candidate construction is wrong.
detail: Triplet loss looks at just one `(anchor, positive, negative)` triple at a time and stops pushing the moment `d(a, n) > d(a, p) + margin`—so if 95% of random triplets are already easy, 95% of your compute produces exact zero gradient! InfoNCE compares against *all* `N − 1` negatives simultaneously via softmax, automatically giving larger gradient weight to whichever negatives currently score highest.
example: If d(a,p)=0.2, d(a,n)=0.6 and margin m=0.3, triplet loss is max(0, 0.2 − 0.6 + 0.3) = 0 (zero learning), whereas InfoNCE still nudges scores cleanly.
follow: When might margin-based losses still be useful (e.g., face verification with a fixed cosine acceptance threshold)?

q: Random, hard and false negatives?
a: Random negatives are often easy. Hard negatives look similar to the query but are actually irrelevant, such as the right product with the wrong version. Mine them using an existing retriever, then filter or label them. A false negative is relevant material mistakenly pushed away.
nuance: Use a mix of difficulty levels, remove duplicates and inspect the hardest cases. A guide model or human labels can filter likely false negatives but are not perfect ground truth. Unclicked impressions are not guaranteed irrelevant.
detail: Start with the meaning of relevance. A non-clicked impression is observed under one exposure policy; a random catalog item may never have been visible. Hard negatives sharpen distinctions but often contain unlabeled positives. Deduplicate known positives in-batch, mix hardness levels, and inspect training versus serving candidate distributions.
example: For a job query, a second suitable job in the same training batch may be a false negative even if only one application was recorded.
follow: How do you mine negatives without using test labels? What changes when popular items dominate batches?

q: Multimodal contrastive learning: CLIP versus SigLIP?
a: CLIP trains separate image and text encoders to land in one shared L2-normalized vector space using **symmetric InfoNCE** across an \(N\times N\) batch grid (every image picks its caption AND every caption picks its image). **SigLIP** replaces that batch-wide softmax competition with independent **pairwise sigmoid binary cross-entropy** on every `(image, text)` cell—removing cross-GPU `AllGather` bottlenecks and working cleanly at smaller batch sizes.
detail: Two interview favorites on CLIP/SigLIP: (1) **Why learnable temperature `τ` needs clamping:** cosine similarities live in `[-1, +1]`; without dividing by `τ ≈ 0.01–0.07`, `exp(1)` vs `exp(0)` can barely reach 73% confidence! CLIP learns `log(1/τ)` directly, clamping max scale to `100` so gradients don't explode early on. (2) **Why SigLIP scales cleaner:** softmax needs the sum over *all* `N` columns on every GPU simultaneously, whereas SigLIP treats diagonal cells as `y=+1` and off-diagonals as `y=−1` with a learned bias `b` (initialized near `-10` since `N²−N` cells are negative!), letting GPUs compute loss in chunks and handle multi-positive matches naturally.

rows: CLIP (Symmetric InfoNCE)
Row-wise + column-wise N-way softmax over scaled cosines.
Strong hard-negative competition, but prefers huge global batches (32k+) and full cross-GPU denominator sync.
SigLIP (Pairwise Sigmoid)
Independent logistic loss on every (i, j) pair with learned scale & negative bias.
Works well from modest (2k–4k) to huge batches, lower memory/comms overhead, and cleaner multi-positive handling.

notation: \(u_i, v_j\) are unit image/text vectors; \(z_{ij}=+1\) on matching diagonal \(i=j\) and \(-1\) off-diagonal; \(t = \exp(t')\) is learned inverse temperature and \(b\) is learned bias.
example: In a 4,096 batch, 16,773,120 pairs are negative and only 4,096 are positive! Initializing SigLIP's bias to b = −10 starts initial loss low instead of wasting early steps just learning that 99.98% of random pairs don't match.
follow: How does CLIP perform zero-shot classification on a brand-new dataset without training a linear head, and why does prompt phrasing (`'a photo of a {label}'`) matter?

q: Cosine similarity versus dot product versus Euclidean distance?
a: Cosine measures pure angle (ignoring vector length), dot product multiplies angle by lengths, and on L2-normalized vectors all three produce the exact same ranking (`‖u−v‖² = 2 − 2uᵀv`). **In practice:** **L2-normalize vectors and use inner product (= cosine)** by default for text/RAG/CLIP retrieval so long documents don't win via big norms; keep **unnormalized dot product** in two-tower recommenders when vector magnitude intentionally encodes item popularity/confidence.
formula:
\cos(u,v) = \frac{u^\top v}{\lVert u\rVert_2\,\lVert v\rVert_2}
\lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert v\rVert_2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lVert u-v\rVert_2^2=2-2u^\top v
nuance: A zero vector needs an explicit policy before normalization. Norms may encode useful confidence or popularity, so removing them changes the task. Match the ANN index metric to the trained scoring function.
detail: Memorize one geometric identity: when two vectors have length 1 (`‖u‖₂ = ‖v‖₂ = 1`), `‖u − v‖₂² = 1 + 1 − 2(uᵀv) = 2(1 − cos(u,v))`. That means L2-normalizing embeddings upfront turns cosine search, dot-product search and Euclidean nearest-neighbor search into the exact same ranking! Keep unnormalized dot product only when vector length intentionally encodes item popularity or confidence.
example: Item A `[10, 10]` (norm 14.1) vs. Item B `[1, 0]` (norm 1) for query `[1, 0]`: dot product picks A (`10 > 1`) due to sheer length; cosine picks B (`1.0 > 0.707`) for exact directional match.
follow: If you train a two-tower model with cosine loss (normalized vectors) but build an unnormalized inner-product ANN index on raw outputs, what goes wrong?

q: Pooling, collapse and embedding evaluation?
a: Convert token states to one vector using a trained CLS representation, masked mean pooling or another task-trained pooler. Mean pooling must ignore padding. Collapse maps unrelated inputs to nearly identical vectors; inspect vector norms, variance and similarity distributions.
nuance: Unsupervised SimCSE uses independent dropout views of the same sentence as positives. Its results illustrate why the training signal and noise matter; pooling an arbitrary language model is not equivalent to training a sentence encoder. Evaluate retrieval by domain, length, language and rare entities, then check ANN recall against exact search.
detail: Mean pooling averages valid token vectors; max pooling keeps the largest value per dimension; CLS/last-token pooling depends on the training setup. Mask padding and define empty-input behavior. Collapse means distinct inputs map to indistinguishable vectors; check variance, pairwise similarities and retrieval quality rather than vector norms alone.
example: Tokens [-5,-3] with padding 0 have real max -3, not 0. Mask padded values with negative infinity before max; return a documented fallback for an all-padding row.
follow: Why does padding change a naive mean? Which pooling choices fit a causal encoder?

q: How do you choose exact search, HNSW or IVF?
a: Exact search checks every vector (100% recall); HNSW walks a multi-layer RAM graph; IVF-PQ clusters vectors and compresses them to save memory. **In practice:** use **exact matmul / pgvector flat** under ~50k–100k vectors (zero index headaches, trivial SQL/ACL filtering!); **HNSW** from ~100k–10M+ when RAM fits and you need <10 ms high recall; **IVF-PQ or DiskANN** past ~50M–1B vectors when uncompressed graphs blow past RAM or heavy filters fragment HNSW.
detail: HNSW navigates a graph; IVF searches selected coarse clusters and may use compressed vectors. Increasing search effort generally improves recall at additional cost. Evaluate filtered queries explicitly: post-filtering can leave too few results. Keep exact top-k on a representative sample as an approximation reference, distinct from relevance labels.
example: If exact embedding search finds the desired item but ANN does not, investigate index/search settings. If neither finds it, the embedding or labels are more likely at fault.
follow: What changes when permissions filter out 99% of candidates? How do updates affect index choice?

q: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise losses: when would you use each?
a: Pointwise predicts each item's independent probability; pairwise compares `(winner, loser)` pairs; listwise scores a whole candidate slate together. **In practice:** use **pointwise BCE** for ads and multi-task home feeds because you need calibrated probabilities (`pCTR`, `pCVR`, `pHide`) to plug into expected-dollar/utility formulas; use **pairwise / listwise (LambdaMART, listwise softmax)** for pure search relevance where only top-K order (`NDCG@10`) matters.
detail: BCE is convenient for probabilistic heads and expected-value ranking. Pairwise logistic loss increases the positive-minus-negative score margin, but gives no calibrated click probability. Listwise softmax compares candidates within a query; candidate sampling and relevance normalization define the task. Lambda-style methods weight ranking updates using changes in a ranking metric.
example: For preferred item score 2 and other score 1, pairwise logistic loss is log(1+exp(−1))≈0.313. Equal scores give log(2)≈0.693.
follow: Why can a high AUC model have weak NDCG@10? What happens when every pair comes from a different query?
notation: s+ and s− are scores for the preferred and less-preferred item within the same context.

q: What does position bias do, and when does IPS help?
a: Clicks depend on exposure as well as relevance. Inverse propensity weighting gives more weight to outcomes observed under less likely exposure, under explicit identification and overlap assumptions.
detail: Distinguish examination propensity for position bias from action probabilities used in off-policy evaluation. Both require a credible probability model and support: zero-probability events cannot be recovered by weighting. Small propensities cause high variance; clipping stabilizes estimates but introduces bias. Randomized traffic can help estimate or validate the correction.
example: An observed event with propensity 0.1 receives weight 10, versus weight 2 at propensity 0.5. One poorly estimated rare event can dominate the objective.
follow: How would you estimate propensities? Why is adding position as a feature not a complete correction?

q: How do multi-task models and utility functions interact?
a: A multi-task model predicts several outcomes; a utility function decides how to combine them. Shared representation learning and business trade-offs are separate choices.
detail: Shared layers can transfer signal from frequent clicks to sparse applications, but conflicting gradients can hurt a task. Compare per-task and joint models; inspect loss weights and missing-label masks. Ranking utility might combine calibrated outcomes with values and penalties. Tune product weights through experiments with guardrails; do not assume each head should have equal importance.
example: A job ranker could predict click, application and hide. Maximizing clicks alone may promote attractive but unsuitable listings.
follow: How would you detect negative transfer? Why are arbitrary logits unsafe to sum as expected values?

q: Multi-task ranking: Shared-Bottom versus MMoE versus PLE?
a: Sharing one trunk across click, watch-time and conversion heads helps data-scarce tasks borrow representations, but when tasks partially conflict (clickbaity items boost CTR while hurting dwell/hides), a shared trunk suffers **negative transfer** (improving one head degrades another—the 'seesaw'). **MMoE** gives each task its own input-dependent gate over multiple shared experts, and **PLE** separates explicitly *shared* experts from *task-private* experts.
detail: Think of Shared-Bottom as forcing a sprinter and a marathoner to follow the exact same coach 100% of the time; MMoE hires 6 specialist coaches (experts) and gives each athlete a personal router (softmax gate over the input `x`) deciding which coaches to listen to for *this* specific user-item pair; PLE guarantees each athlete also keeps 1–2 private coaches that the other task's gradients can never corrupt! Also watch **selection bias** in conversions: `pCVR` trained only on clicked items sees a biased subset—ESMM-style `pCTCVR = pCTR × pCVR` trains across the entire impression space.

rows: Shared-Bottom
One shared MLP trunk → thin task towers.
Fastest and great when tasks are tightly correlated; seesaws badly when gradients conflict.
MMoE (Multi-gate MoE)
K shared expert MLPs + one softmax gate per task.
Handles loosely correlated tasks smoothly; experts can still collapse or tangle without private capacity.
PLE (Progressive Layered Extraction)
Explicit task-specific experts + shared experts per level.
Strongest insulation against the multi-task seesaw at slightly higher serving compute.

example: On a feed predicting `p(click)` (5% rate) and `p(share)` (0.05% rate), clicks are 100× denser: without MMoE/PLE or gradient balancing, click gradients completely overwrite the trunk.
follow: Why must training loss weights (`L = w₁ L_click + w₂ L_hide`) be tuned separately from the serving business formula (`Score = α·p_click − β·p_hide`)?

sources.title: Sumit's Diary: Multi-task learning in RecSys

q: Deep dive: train and serve a two-tower retriever
a: Encode query/user context and items separately into a shared space, train positives to score above negatives, precompute item vectors, and retrieve candidates with a compatible index.
detail: Choose labels and temporal splits first. Query-only features belong in the query tower; query-item interactions cannot be precomputed in the item tower. Explain the contrastive score matrix and temperature, false-negative masking, and negative sampling distribution. Evaluate exact retrieval to separate representation quality from ANN approximation, then measure end-to-end ranking and online outcomes. Version both towers and index together.
example: With B query-positive pairs, query_vectors @ item_vectors.T yields B×B scores. Diagonal entries are positives only if the batch construction actually pairs row i with item i.
follow: Why is a cross-encoder too costly for catalog-wide retrieval? When are off-diagonal items also positives? How would you serve a new item?

q: What is a tokenizer, and what is its goal?
a: A tokenizer converts text into a sequence of discrete token IDs that a model can consume. It balances vocabulary size, sequence length and coverage of rare strings or languages. Tokens are not necessarily words, characters or semantic units; the embedding lookup happens after tokenization.
nuance: The pipeline can include normalization, pre-tokenization, subword segmentation and special tokens. Decoding recovers text under that pipeline’s rules; normalization can discard information. IDs are arbitrary vocabulary indices, not numerical measures of similarity.
detail: Character-level tokenization has tiny vocab (~256) so zero unknown words, but turns a short paragraph into 2,000 tiny tokens—blowing up quadratic attention cost! Whole-word tokenization keeps sequences short, but needs millions of vocabulary rows and still chokes on typos, code identifiers (`parseHttpHeader`) or new slang. Subword tokenizers hit the sweet spot: common words stay 1 token (`' the'`), rare words split into meaningful pieces (`'token' + 'ization'`).
example: In a 100k BPE vocab, `'apple'` is 1 token, whereas a rare chemical `'methylprednisolone'` splits into 4–5 reusable subword chunks instead of becoming `<UNK>`.
follow: Why do many LLMs struggle with character-level tasks like counting `'r'`s in `'strawberry'` or exact multi-digit arithmetic?

q: BPE versus WordPiece versus Unigram?
a: BPE merges frequent adjacent byte/char pairs, WordPiece merges high-pointwise-mutual-information pairs, and Unigram prunes down a large probabilistic vocabulary. **In practice:** **byte-level BPE** is the universal choice when building or using modern causal LLMs (GPT, Llama, Qwen, Claude) because raw byte fallback guarantees zero `<UNK>` tokens on code, math or emojis; **WordPiece / Unigram** show up mainly via pretrained BERT/DeBERTa/T5 encoders.

rows: BPE
Repeatedly merge frequent adjacent symbol pairs; apply learned merges.
Byte-level BPE starts from bytes and can represent arbitrary text without an unknown token.
WordPiece
Common accounts score merges by association relative to piece frequencies; tokenize with longest matching pieces.
Greedy segmentation is different from replaying BPE merges; exact training implementations vary.
Unigram
Begin with a candidate vocabulary and prune under a probabilistic model; choose a likely segmentation.
Can support multiple segmentations and sampling rather than one fixed merge path.

nuance: SentencePiece is a tokenizer toolkit, not a synonym for Unigram; it supports BPE too. Byte fallback is a configuration choice, not a guarantee of every subword tokenizer.
detail: Intuition: BPE builds bottom-up by greedily gluing whichever adjacent pair appears most often ('i' + 'n' → 'in' → 'ing'), even if both pieces were just common letters on their own. WordPiece glues pairs that appear together more often than chance given their individual counts (count(ab) / (count(a)·count(b))). Unigram works top-down: start with a huge candidate dictionary and iteratively prune pieces whose removal barely hurts corpus log-likelihood.
example: If 'e' and 's' are common everywhere, raw BPE merges 'es' early; WordPiece prefers merging a high-affinity pair like 'qu' where 'q' almost always precedes 'u'.
follow: Why did GPT and Llama adopt byte-level BPE instead of character-level BPE?

q: Why does tokenization affect cost and quality?
a: More tokens mean less text fits into a fixed context window and more attention and decoding work. A larger vocabulary can shorten sequences but enlarges embedding/output tables and softmax work. Different languages, code and numbers may fragment very differently.
nuance: Count tokens with the model’s exact tokenizer, including chat-template special tokens. Token IDs and embedding rows must stay aligned; swapping tokenizers is not a harmless preprocessing change. Compare perplexity only with compatible tokenization and evaluation conventions.
detail: Token fertility (tokens per word/character) directly taxes both latency and context capacity: if Language B takes 3× more tokens than English to express the same sentence, users in Language B pay 3× slower decode latency and fit 3× fewer documents into the same 32k context window! Likewise, splitting `'123456'` inconsistently into `'12' + '345' + '6'` makes arithmetic harder than consistent digit grouping.
example: At 50 tokens/sec decode speed, a 200-word answer taking 250 English tokens finishes in 5s; at 750 tokens in an under-represented script, the same answer takes 15s.
follow: If you fine-tune an English LLM on biomedical code/data full of domain symbols, when is extending the tokenizer worth the pain of resizing and retraining the embedding matrix?

q: Causal language modeling versus masked language modeling?
a: Causal LMs predict the next token left-to-right; masked LMs predict hidden tokens using both left and right context simultaneously. **In practice:** reach for **masked bidirectional encoders** (DeBERTa, ModernBERT, BGE) whenever you need cheap, sub-20 ms high-QPS classification, NER, embeddings or cross-encoder reranking; use **causal decoder LLMs** for generation, synthesis, tool calling and zero/few-shot tasks.
notation: The prefix contains only earlier tokens. N counts scored tokens, excluding ignored padding; exponentiation assumes natural logarithms.
nuance: At generation time, the model conditions on its own outputs, so errors can compound. Encoder–decoder models use bidirectional source attention and causal target attention, with cross-attention connecting them.
detail: Use a simple division of labor: **masked LMs** (BERT/DeBERTa) peek at both left and right context at once, making them compact, fast powerhouses for classification, NER, bi-encoder embeddings and cross-encoder reranking. **Causal LMs** (GPT/Llama/Claude) mask future tokens so all `T` next-token predictions train in a single parallel forward pass—and can generate open-ended text, code and tool calls autoregressively.
example: In `'The bank by the [MASK] flooded'`, a bidirectional encoder uses `'flooded'` on the right to know `'bank'` means riverbank, not Chase Bank.
follow: What is exposure bias (teacher forcing vs. autoregressive rollout), and why can tiny per-token errors snowball over a 500-token generation?

q: Derive attention and shapes.
a: For input X with shape (B, T, E), project Q and K to \((B,T,d_k)\), and V to \((B,T,d_v)\). Scores and attention weights have shape (B, T, T). Softmax runs across key positions; weighted values produce \((B,T,d_v)\).
follow: Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?
notation: Transpose only the final two axes of K. M is an additive mask: 0 for allowed pairs, −∞ for masked pairs.
nuance: If query/key coordinates are independent with unit variance, their dot product has variance dₖ. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps initial logits from growing with head width and saturating softmax.
detail: Intuition in 3 database words: every token broadcasts a **Query** ('what am I looking for?'), a **Key** ('what label describes me?'), and a **Value** ('what payload do I hand over if matched?'). Dot-multiplying `Q` with `Kᵀ` scores every `(query, key)` pair; dividing by `√d_k` stops wide vectors from producing huge dot products that push softmax into `[0, 0, 1, 0]` saturation with near-zero gradients; softmax turns scores into weights summing to 1; multiplying by `V` blends the matched payloads.
example: If Q and K have d_k=64 independent N(0,1) entries, Q·K is a sum of 64 unit-variance products → variance = 64, std = 8! Dividing by √64 = 8 brings logits back to std = 1.

q: Causal versus padding masks?
a: Causal masks prevent attending to future tokens; padding masks exclude padding keys. Apply masks to logits before softmax, typically with negative infinity. Define behavior for fully masked rows to avoid NaNs.
follow: Why does multiplying logits by zero not mask them?
detail: Classic live-coding bug: multiplying masked attention scores by `0` instead of setting them to `-∞`! Why? Because `exp(0) = 1`, which gives padded or future tokens positive weight in softmax! Setting disallowed positions to `-∞` before softmax makes `exp(-∞) = 0`. One crucial edge case: if left-padding leaves a query row with *all* keys masked (`[-∞, -∞, ...]`), shifting by max yields `-∞ - (-∞) = NaN`—guard all-masked rows with `0` before softmax and zero out their weights after.
example: Scores `[2.0, 99.0]` where position 1 is PAD: multiplying by `[1, 0]` gives `softmax([2.0, 0.0]) = [0.88, 0.12]` (12% leaked from PAD!); setting `-∞` gives `softmax([2.0, -∞]) = [1.0, 0.0]`.

q: What makes a Transformer block?
a: Multi-head attention combines learned attention subspaces; a position-wise feed-forward network transforms features. Residual connections and normalization stabilize depth. Position information is required because unpositioned self-attention is permutation equivariant.
follow: Contrast encoder self-attention, decoder masked attention and cross-attention.
notation: This is pre-norm, omitting dropout. The attention output projection returns to the residual width. FFN typically expands then contracts each token’s features.
nuance: Pre-norm keeps an identity residual path and often eases optimization at depth. Post-norm normalizes after the residual addition. Neither ordering replaces positional information.
detail: Notice the clean separation of jobs inside every block: **Attention** is the *only* place tokens talk to other tokens across the sequence (`communication`), while the **FFN** runs identically and independently on each token vector (`per-token computation / key-value memory`), usually expanding width ~3–4× before projecting back. Residual streams + Pre-RMSNorm wrap both sublayers so depth stays trainable.
example: For hidden size D=4096, classic MHA has 4×D² = 67M params (`Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo`) while a 4D FFN has 2×D×4D = 134M params—roughly two-thirds of a dense Transformer's weights live in its FFNs!

q: Self-attention versus cross-attention; encoder versus decoder?
a: Self-attention mixes tokens within one sequence; cross-attention lets target queries attend over a separate source memory. **In practice:** **decoder-only causal self-attention** is the standard for modern LLMs and agents (prompt + output share one KV cache and weight stack); **encoder–decoder / cross-attention** stays useful when encoding a heavy non-text modality once (like Whisper audio frames or ViT image patches) and decoding short text.
nuance: “Decoder-only” models have causal self-attention but typically no encoder cross-attention. Multi-head attention uses multiple projected subspaces, concatenates head outputs, then projects back to model width.
detail: In cross-attention, queries come from the target sequence `(B, T_q, d_k)` while keys and values come from the source memory `(B, T_k, d_k)`—so the attention map is rectangular `(B, H, T_q, T_k)` and softmax still normalizes over the `T_k` source keys! That's how Whisper (text queries attending to audio frames) or encoder–decoder translation works, whereas modern chat LLMs simply concatenate `[prompt_tokens, generated_tokens]` into one decoder-only causal self-attention stream.
example: Generating 10 English caption tokens (`T_q=10`) over 256 ViT image patches (`T_k=256`) produces a `10 × 256` cross-attention weight matrix per head.
follow: Why did most general-purpose LLMs converge on decoder-only causal architectures rather than encoder–decoder?

q: Absolute positions versus RoPE?
a: Absolute embeddings add a fixed position vector at layer 0; RoPE rotates Query and Key pairs by position angle at every attention layer so dot products depend only on relative token distance. **In practice:** **RoPE** is the universal default in modern LLMs because it generalizes cleanly to long contexts (32k–128k+ via RoPE scaling); **learned absolute embeddings** remain completely fine for short fixed-length encoders (512-token BERT, ViT image patches, or 50-event user history towers).
nuance: RoPE does not by itself guarantee reliable extrapolation beyond training length. Changing position scaling, extending the context and validating long-distance retrieval are separate considerations.
detail: If you shuffle the words in a bag without positional info, self-attention produces the exact same outputs (just shuffled)—it is permutation-equivariant! Learned absolute embeddings add `pos_vec[t]` at layer 0, which struggles when test prompts exceed training length and blurs relative distance deep in the stack. **RoPE** instead rotates each `(even, odd)` pair of Query and Key coordinates like clock hands by angle `t · θ_i`: when `Q_m` dots with `K_n`, only the angle difference `(m − n) · θ_i` survives!
example: Rotating Q at token 10 by 100° and K at token 7 by 70° gives the exact same dot product as rotating Q at token 3 by 30° and K at token 0 by 0°—only the 3-token gap (30°) matters.
follow: During KV-cached decoding at token position 500, why must you pass explicit position index `500` to RoPE instead of `0`?

q: What does KV caching save?
a: During autoregressive decoding, reuse old keys and values instead of recomputing them. Each new query still attends to the available context. Cache memory per token is 2×layers×KV_heads×head_dim×bytes, per sequence; query heads may differ under GQA.
follow: Why cache K and V but usually not old Q?
notation: \(B\) = batch size, \(T\) = cached tokens, \(L\) = layers, \(H_{\mathrm{KV}}\) = KV heads, \(d_h\) = head width, \(b_{\mathrm{elem}}\) = bytes per stored element. Excludes weights, activations and allocator overhead.
nuance: Old Q is unnecessary because only the new token’s output is being computed. Cache reuse requires a matching prefix, model and position/mask convention; training usually processes full sequences without this decode cache.
detail: Without a KV cache, generating a 1,000-token answer recomputes `K` and `V` for tokens `1..t` at every single step (`1 + 2 + ... + 1000 ≈ 500,000` token passes—quadratic!). Because causal masking guarantees token 5's `K` and `V` never change when token 6 arrives, caching past `K` and `V` turns each new decode step into projecting *just 1 new token* (`q_t, k_t, v_t`) and attending `q_t` over cached keys (`O(t)` instead of `O(t²)`). The catch: that cache lives in precious GPU HBM!
example: Llama-style 8B model (`L=32, H_kv=8, d_h=128`, BF16 = 2 bytes): `2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes ≈ 128 KB/token` → ~0.5 GB for one 4k sequence, or ~16 GB across a batch of 32!

q: Attention cost and FlashAttention?
a: Dense attention interactions scale quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention uses tiled exact attention to reduce memory traffic and avoid materializing the full attention matrix; it does not make dense attention mathematically linear-time.
follow: How do prefill and one-token decode differ?
nuance: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel; decode produces one token at a time and often becomes memory-bandwidth limited. Dense prefill attention is \(O(T^2d)\); each decode step attends over T cached tokens in \(O(Td)\) per head.
detail: Modern GPUs compute matrix multiplies 10–20× faster than they can read/write bytes to main GPU memory (HBM). Naive attention writes the huge `T × T` score matrix out to slow HBM, reads it back for softmax, writes weights back to HBM, and reads them again to multiply `V`! **FlashAttention** loads small blocks of `Q, K, V` into tiny, ultra-fast on-chip SRAM and uses *online softmax* (tracking running max and sum across tiles) to compute the **exact same output** (zero approximation!) without ever materializing the `T × T` matrix in HBM—slashing memory from `O(T²)` to `O(T)` and giving 2–4× wall-clock speedup.
example: At T=32,768 and H=32 heads in FP16, a single layer's materialized T×T matrix takes `32 × 32768² × 2 bytes = 68.7 GB` (instant OOM!), whereas FlashAttention needs only a few megabytes.

q: MHA versus MQA versus GQA?
a: MHA gives every query head its own KV head; MQA shares 1 KV head across all queries; GQA shares 1 KV head per group of 4–8 query heads. **In practice:** **GQA** is the production standard for virtually all modern 7B–400B LLMs (slashing KV-cache RAM and decode bandwidth 4–8× with near-zero quality loss); **MHA** still lives in small bidirectional encoders that don't use KV caches, while **MLA** powers giant MoEs squeezing KV memory even further.
nuance: GQA reduces KV storage, not the number of query heads. It still attends to explicit previous token positions; it is not a recurrent compression of the whole sequence.
detail: During token-by-token decoding, the GPU stalls waiting to stream cached `K` and `V` tensors out of HBM memory for every generated token. **GQA** is the Goldilocks fix: keep all `H_q` query heads so the model retains rich multi-subspace queries, but let groups of `g = H_q / H_kv` query heads share one `K` and `V` head—cutting KV-cache RAM and HBM memory reads by `g×` with virtually zero accuracy drop. (**MLA**, used in DeepSeek, goes further by compressing KV into a shared low-rank latent vector cached per token.)

rows: MHA (Multi-Head)
H_kv = H_q (1 per query head)
Highest KV cache footprint; decode quickly hits HBM bandwidth wall.
GQA (Grouped-Query)
1 < H_kv < H_q (e.g., 8 KV for 32 Q)
4×–8× smaller KV cache & faster decode with near-MHA quality; modern standard.
MQA (Multi-Query)
H_kv = 1 across all query heads
Smallest simple KV cache, but more noticeable quality drop unless trained/adapted carefully.
MLA (Multi-Head Latent)
Compressed low-rank latent c_t^(KV)
Even smaller KV cache than GQA at stronger quality, with extra projection math.

example: Shifting from MHA (32 KV heads) to GQA (8 KV heads) shrinks KV cache 4×, letting the same GPU serve 4× larger concurrent batch size or 4× longer context!
follow: In PyTorch code, how do 8 KV heads broadcast or repeat to match 32 Query heads before `Q @ K.transpose(-1, -2)`?

q: Prefill, decode and batching: where does latency come from?
a: Prefill processes the prompt; decode generates subsequent tokens with cached attention state. Track time to first token, time per output token and total request latency separately.
detail: Long prompts increase prefill work and cache occupancy. Decode often faces memory-bandwidth limits at small batches; batching can improve utilization but adds queueing and memory pressure. Continuous batching admits and retires requests as they progress. Prefix caching reuses compatible prompt-prefix computation, while output caching reuses a response; their correctness conditions differ.
example: An agent making eight serial model calls may be slower than one call with the same total tokens because every call adds scheduling, prefill and network overhead.
follow: How does a long output affect concurrency? When can a larger batch hurt p95 latency?

q: Fine-tuning, LoRA or RAG?
a: RAG injects fresh external facts at query time; LoRA trains tiny low-rank adapter matrices to change model behavior/style; full fine-tuning updates every weight. **In practice:** always start with **prompting + RAG** when facts update, permissions matter or citations are required; add **LoRA SFT** to lock in strict formatting, domain tone/routing or distilling an expensive prompt into a fast 8B model; reserve **full fine-tuning** for heavy continued pretraining.
follow: What evidence would justify fine-tuning? What must stay in an external data source?
nuance: LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, but the frozen base weights still need to be stored or quantized. RAG cannot fix a model that consistently ignores supplied evidence; fine-tuning cannot guarantee fresh facts.
detail: Diagnose the failure first: unavailable or changing facts suggest retrieval; output conventions or task behavior may benefit from supervised examples; a poor prompt or tool contract should be fixed directly. RAG and adaptation can be combined. LoRA changes which parameters are trained, not whether the task is retrieval or generation.
example: For current account balances, query an authorized system of record. For consistently producing a validated domain-specific schema, improve prompting and measure whether SFT adds value.

q: Pretraining versus SFT versus preference optimization?
a: Pretraining learns broad patterns from a large corpus. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns desired responses from demonstrations. Preference optimization uses comparisons or rewards to favor better responses; DPO learns directly from chosen/rejected pairs, while RL methods optimize rewards through policy updates.
nuance: Better preference scores do not guarantee factuality or task success. The preference data, rubric and reward model can be biased or exploitable; keep held-out task evaluations and inspect regressions.
detail: Why isn't pretraining enough? Because a raw pretrained model trained on internet text treats `'How do I fix a leaky faucet?'` as the start of a quiz page and happily outputs `'Question 2: How do I wire a lamp?'`! **SFT** teaches the assistant *format and helpfulness* by imitating curated `(prompt, ideal_response)` demos. **Preference optimization (DPO / RLHF / GRPO)** teaches *judgment*: it is often much easier to grade or compare two candidate answers (or run a code unit test) than to write a single gold human essay for every hard prompt.
example: Pretraining learns Python syntax and libraries; SFT learns to answer coding questions politely with markdown blocks; RL/GRPO with test execution teaches the model to catch subtle off-by-one bugs.
follow: When can aggressive SFT or DPO make a model *more* confident in hallucinations ('alignment tax' / sycophancy)?

q: Temperature versus top-k versus top-p sampling?
a: Temperature scales logit sharpness before softmax; top-k caps candidate count; top-p (nucleus) dynamically keeps just enough top tokens to cover probability mass `p`. **In practice:** set **`temperature = 0`** for deterministic JSON extraction, SQL, classification and evals; use **`temperature ≈ 0.6–0.8` + `top_p ≈ 0.9–0.95`** (leaving `top_k` off or wide) for natural chat/writing; and use **`temperature ≈ 0.7–1.0`** when sampling diverse candidates for best-of-N or RL (GRPO).
nuance: Greedy decoding takes the maximum directly rather than dividing by zero. Sampling temperature is a decoding choice; contrastive-loss temperature shapes a training objective. Reducing randomness does not guarantee truth or globally optimal sequences.
detail: Even at low temperature (`T = 0.7`), standard softmax assigns tiny nonzero probability to 100,000 absurd tail tokens—over 1,000 tokens, summing 100,000 tiny tails can still sample nonsense! **Top-k** chops off everything past rank `k`, which fails in both directions: if 1 token has 99% probability, `k=50` still lets 49 weird tokens in; if 100 creative words tie at 1%, `k=50` cuts half off arbitrarily. **Top-p (nucleus)** adapts dynamically: keep just enough top tokens to cover 90–95% of probability mass (1 token when certain, 80 tokens when open-ended), then renormalize.
example: For `'2 + 2 ='` where `' 4'` has p=0.98, `top_p=0.95` keeps ONLY `' 4'` (size 1); for `'Write a story starting with'` where probabilities are flat, `top_p=0.95` keeps dozens of valid openings.
follow: When should you set `temperature = 0` (greedy), and why do best-of-N / RL rollouts require `temperature > 0`?

q: LoRA versus QLoRA versus full fine-tuning: what uses memory?
a: Full fine-tuning pays ~16 bytes/param for weights, grads and AdamW states; LoRA freezes BF16 base weights (`2B/param`) and trains tiny rank-`r` adapters; QLoRA quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit `NF4` (`~0.5B/param`). **In practice:** **BF16 LoRA** is the default workhorse for 90% of fine-tunes (fast kernels, merges cleanly into base weights for zero serving overhead); use **QLoRA** only when VRAM is tight on a single GPU; use **full fine-tuning** for large mid-training domain shifts on multi-GPU clusters.
detail: Separate base weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations and temporary buffers in the memory budget. Adapter training reduces trainable state but long sequences still consume activation memory. Checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory. Quantization introduces approximation; benchmark quality and supported serving kernels.
example: For a d×d matrix, rank-r LoRA has 2dr parameters instead of d² for its update. With d=4096 and r=8, that is 65,536 versus 16,777,216.
follow: Why can LoRA still run out of memory? What does merging an adapter change at serving time?
notation: A has shape (r,d_in), B has shape (d_out,r); W0 is frozen.

q: How does knowledge distillation help production?
a: Train a smaller student to reproduce useful teacher behavior, then validate the quality-cost trade-off on the real task. Distillation can target probabilities, representations or generated examples.
detail: Soft targets convey relative preferences beyond the winning class. For classification, a common loss combines hard-label cross entropy with temperature-scaled teacher/student KL. Generated-label distillation also needs filtering and coverage checks: the student inherits teacher errors and may miss rare cases.
example: An expensive reranker labels candidate pairs offline; a small model learns to score them online. Evaluate independently of the teacher’s labels before shipping.
follow: Why use temperature in soft-target distillation? How do you keep the teacher from contaminating evaluation?
notation: λ is the loss weight; T is temperature; p_t and p_s are teacher and student distributions.

q: SFT versus DPO versus online RL: what data do they need?
a: SFT imitates `(prompt, gold_response)` demos; DPO contrasts offline `(chosen, rejected)` pairs; online RL (PPO/GRPO) grades live model rollouts with a reward/verifier. **In practice:** run **SFT** first to teach format and baseline behavior; use **DPO** as the simplest offline way to polish tone, style and human preference rankings without RL infra; use **online RL (GRPO)** when you have a deterministic verifier (unit tests, math/SQL execution, schema/state sandboxes) where exploration beats human demos.
detail: SFT demonstrations need correct behavior and representative coverage. Preference pairs must compare responses to the same prompt and may encode annotator biases. Online rollouts can explore new behavior but require reward validation, rollout infrastructure and careful evaluation for reward exploitation. DPO is not a substitute for fixing missing evidence or an unreliable tool.
example: If preferences reward long answers, both preference learning and reward optimization may increase verbosity without improving correctness.
follow: What would make a preference pair ambiguous? How would you detect reward hacking?

q: What makes a good supervised fine-tuning dataset?
a: Use representative, correct input-output examples with a stable task definition. Deduplicate and split by underlying task/source before generating variants, then evaluate held-out behavior.
detail: Choose a loss mask appropriate to the task: instruction tuning commonly supervises assistant output rather than treating user text as the target. Preserve tool schemas and valid argument/result relationships for tool-use examples. Mix coverage deliberately, audit synthetic labels, and compare against the unadapted model and prompting baseline.
example: Twenty paraphrases of one source document split across train and test exaggerate generalization. Group by source or task family before augmentation.
follow: How would you detect memorization? Which failures suggest missing data versus an unsuitable objective?

q: Deep dive: how modern 2025–2026 LLMs differ from the 2017 Transformer
a: Walk through five clean upgrades over the original 2017 paper: **(1) Decoder-only + Pre-RMSNorm** for stable deep gradients, **(2) RoPE (+ QK-Norm)** for relative positions without length walls, **(3) GQA or MLA** to slash KV-cache memory during decode, **(4) SwiGLU 3-matrix FFNs** for stronger expressiveness per FLOP, and **(5) Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** to scale knowledge capacity (`total params`) without scaling per-token latency (`active params`).
detail: Explain *why* each change happened rather than reciting buzzwords: Post-LayerNorm required fragile warmup or diverged at depth → **Pre-RMSNorm** leaves an untouched residual highway and skips mean subtraction; **QK-Norm** applies RMSNorm to queries and keys right before attention so massive scale/long-context logits don't spike; **SwiGLU** uses 3 projections (`gate, up, down`), so hidden width shrinks from `4d` to `(8/3)d` to keep total FFN parameter count constant at `8d²`; and **Sparse MoE** replaces one giant FFN with `E` smaller expert FFNs where a lightweight router activates only top-`k` (e.g., 8 of 256) experts per token—giving 200B+ knowledge capacity at ~20B active FLOP cost, provided router load-balancing prevents every token from crowding into 2 experts!
notation: \(\operatorname{SiLU}(z) = z\,\sigma(z)\); with \(d_{\mathrm{ff}} = \frac{8}{3}d\), three \(d \times d_{\mathrm{ff}}\) matrices total \(3 \cdot d \cdot \frac{8}{3}d = 8d^2\) parameters (matching a classic 2-matrix \(4d\) FFN).
example: A 64-expert MoE activating top-2 experts per token has ~8× the total FFN RAM requirement of a dense model (all 64 experts must sit in GPU memory!), yet runs roughly the same FLOPs per single token as the dense model.
follow: Why is a Sparse MoE great for high-throughput batched cloud serving, yet painful on a single laptop GPU during batch-1 decoding?

q: Where does GPU memory go in training (the 16-byte rule), and what is the Roofline limit?
a: In standard mixed-precision AdamW training, static model state alone costs roughly **16 bytes per parameter** (`2B` BF16 weights + `2B` BF16 gradients + `12B` FP32 master weights, momentum \(m\) and variance \(v\))—before adding activations! And speed is governed by **arithmetic intensity** (FLOPs divided by HBM bytes moved): large-batch matrix multiplies are *compute-bound*, while batch-1 token decoding is *memory-bandwidth-bound*.
detail: Two mental-math rules that win systems interviews immediately: (1) **Why FP32 master weights?** In BF16 (only 7 mantissa bits!), a tiny learning-rate update like `w − 1e-4 · grad = 1.0 − 0.0001` rounds straight back to `1.000` (zero learning!) unless accumulated in a 4-byte FP32 master copy. On top of that `16Ψ` static budget, activations grow with `Batch × Seq × Layers × Hidden`; **activation checkpointing** saves only layer boundaries during forward and recomputes inside each layer during backward (~33% extra compute for massive memory savings). (2) **Roofline:** an H100 does ~990 TFLOPS (BF16) on ~3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth → ridge point `990 / 3.35 ≈ 295 FLOPs/byte`. Any op doing fewer than ~295 math ops per byte fetched from HBM stalls waiting on memory wires!
formula:
\text{Static AdamW RAM} \approx (2_{\text{param}} + 2_{\text{grad}} + 4_{\text{master}} + 4_m + 4_v)\,\Psi = 16\Psi\text{ bytes}
\text{Arithmetic Intensity} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes moved from/to HBM}}
notation: \(\Psi\) = trainable parameter count. For pure BF16 inference, optimizer/gradient/activation-graph states vanish, leaving \(2\Psi\text{ bytes} + \text{KV cache}\).
example: A 7B model needs ~14 GB in BF16 just to run inference (`2 × 7B`), ~112 GB just for static AdamW state (`16 × 7B`, already exceeding one 80 GB GPU before batch=1 activations!), and `Y = xW` at batch=1 moves `2 bytes` per weight to do `2 FLOPs` (`1 FLOP/byte` ≪ 295 → completely bandwidth-bound!).
follow: Why does doubling decode batch size from 1 to 16 barely increase per-step latency on a GPU until you hit the Roofline ridge point?

q: Distributed training: DDP versus FSDP (ZeRO) versus Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism?
a: **DDP** copies the full model onto every GPU and averages gradients (`AllReduce`)—simple until 1 GPU can't hold `16Ψ` bytes. **FSDP / ZeRO** slices optimizer states, gradients and weights across GPUs, fetching each layer just-in-time (`AllGather`). **Tensor Parallelism (TP)** splits individual weight matrices *within* a layer across fast intra-node NVLink GPUs, while **Pipeline Parallelism (PP)** assigns consecutive layer blocks across nodes with microbatches to shrink idle bubbles.
detail: How to combine them ('3D Parallelism') without memorizing trivia: **TP** synchronizes activations *twice inside every single Transformer block* (after MHA and after FFN), so it demands ultra-fast intra-node NVLink (8 GPUs inside 1 box)—never run TP across slow inter-node Ethernet! **PP** only passes boundary activations between layer chunks across nodes, trading communication for a pipeline bubble `(P − 1) / M` shrunk by splitting a batch into `M` microbatches. **FSDP / ZeRO-3** works across nodes by overlapping next-layer `AllGather` with current-layer compute.

rows: DDP
Full 16Ψ replica + 1/N of batch.
One `AllReduce` of gradients per step; fails as soon as model + activations > 1 GPU.
ZeRO-1 / ZeRO-2
Shards optimizer states (ZeRO-1) + gradients (ZeRO-2); keeps weights.
Cuts static RAM from 16Ψ → ~6Ψ (ZeRO-1) → ~4Ψ (ZeRO-2) with almost identical comms to DDP.
FSDP / ZeRO-3
Shards all 16Ψ (weights, grads, opt) by 1/N.
`AllGather` weights before forward & backward + `ReduceScatter` grads (~1.5× DDP comms); scales across nodes.
Tensor Parallel (TP)
1/T slice of each matrix column/row.
`AllReduce` inside *every* layer → keep strictly inside 1 node (NVLink, T ≤ 8).
Pipeline Parallel (PP)
Contiguous slice of layers (e.g., layers 1–8, 9–16).
Point-to-point p2p activations across nodes; needs microbatching (1F1B) to hide idle bubble.

example: Training a 70B model (~1.12 TB static AdamW state) on 64 × 80 GB GPUs: TP=8 inside each 8-GPU node + FSDP=8 across the 8 nodes leaves plenty of HBM per GPU with fast NVLink inside and overlapped Ethernet outside.
follow: When you double cluster size using DDP/FSDP, what happens to your effective global batch size and how should learning rate / warmup adjust?

q: Quantization (FP8, W8A8, W4A16 AWQ/GPTQ) and speculative decoding: how do they speed up serving?
a: Because autoregressive decoding stalls waiting to load weights from GPU memory, **weight-only quantization (`W4A16` like AWQ/GPTQ)** packs weights into 4 bits and dequantizes on-chip to BF16—cutting memory traffic ~4× for a near-linear decode speedup! For heavy prefill or high QPS, **`FP8` / `W8A8`** quantizes *both* weights and activations to unlock 2× faster Tensor Cores. **Speculative decoding** uses a tiny draft model to guess `K` tokens cheaply, then verifies all `K` in *one* parallel forward pass of the target model with **zero change** to the output distribution.
detail: Two crisp nuances interviewers probe: (1) **Why naive `INT8` (`W8A8`) breaks above ~6B params:** Transformers develop a handful of extreme *activation outlier channels* (20–100× larger than normal channels) that stretch a tensor's quantization scale so 99% of normal values round to zero! **AWQ** protects the ~1% of weight channels multiplied by large activations during `W4A16`, while **SmoothQuant / FP8** shifts scale smoothly or uses floating-point exponents that handle wide dynamic range natively. (2) **Why speculative decoding is mathematically lossless:** the target model computes probabilities for all `K` drafted tokens in parallel (compute-rich, like prefill!); rejection sampling accepts token `t` with probability `min(1, p_target / p_draft)` and—on the first rejection—samples a replacement from the residual `norm(max(0, p_target − p_draft))`, guaranteeing the exact target distribution plus 1 bonus token even if every draft guess was rejected!

rows: Weight-only `W4A16` (AWQ / GPTQ)
HBM weight bandwidth + VRAM capacity at small decode batch.
Great for low-concurrency latency; at huge batch sizes dequant overhead can slow compute-bound GEMMs.
`FP8` / `W8A8` (Weight + Activation)
Both HBM traffic AND Tensor Core compute throughput.
Shines on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs for prefill + high-QPS serving; needs outlier-aware scaling for INT8.
KV-cache quantization (FP8/INT4)
Long-context / large-batch KV memory capacity & decode reads.
Calibrate per-head/per-token scales carefully—Key outliers are typically more sensitive than Values.
Speculative decoding
Serial token-by-token decode wall-clock latency.
2–3× lower latency on predictable text (code, JSON, RAG quotes) when GPU has spare FLOPs; less gain at saturated batch sizes.

example: A 70B model in BF16 takes ~140 GB (needs 2 × 80 GB GPUs); `W4A16` AWQ shrinks weights to ~35–40 GB (fits on ONE 80 GB GPU with 40 GB left for KV cache!) and roughly triples batch-1 tokens/sec.
follow: When would Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) not be enough, forcing Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)?

q: How do you separate retrieval failures from generation failures?
a: Evaluate the evidence retrieved, then evaluate the answer given that evidence. Run a gold-context experiment to isolate whether the generator can solve the task with sufficient information.
detail: Build cases with verified supporting spans, conflicting dates, multiple sources and no answer. Score retrieval recall and context coverage separately from answer correctness and citation support. Missing evidence suggests retrieval/chunking problems; wrong answers with complete evidence suggest reasoning, instructions or context-use problems. Gold-context results are diagnostic, not deployment performance.
example: A numerical answer may be fully grounded in an outdated report and still be wrong for the requested quarter. Include version/date correctness in the rubric.
follow: What if the retrieved passage contains the answer but is truncated during context packing? How do you score abstention?

q: How do you validate an LLM judge?
a: Define a narrow rubric, compare judgments against held-out human labels, and investigate systematic disagreements. A model-generated score is a measurement instrument that needs validation.
detail: Use deterministic checks for parsable facts, arithmetic and final state. Use semantic judges for criteria that genuinely require interpretation, with supporting evidence. Blind system identity and randomize pair order; inspect length/style bias. Keep grader versions fixed during comparisons and periodically recheck them as tasks change.
example: A judge rewards a polished answer that omits a required spreadsheet tab. A deterministic tab-existence check catches a failure the prose rubric missed.
follow: How would you handle disagreement among humans? What changes when the judge and candidate are the same model family?

q: How do you measure agent success across repeated runs?
a: Grade the final deliverable or environment state, along with prohibited side effects. Repeat trials to estimate reliability, and report cost and latency for the actual deployment policy.
detail: Separate infrastructure failures from agent errors, but report their user-facing impact too. At-least-one success among k attempts measures a different policy from one-shot success or all-k consistency. A successful transcript claim is not a verified state change. Hold out task templates and compare models on matched, resettable environments.
example: An agent says it saved a report, but no file exists. Outcome validation fails even if its final message sounds perfect.
follow: Who selects the winning attempt in best-of-k? How would you restore the environment between trials?

q: Constrained decoding, hallucinations and reward hacking: what can and cannot be guaranteed?
a: **Constrained decoding** runs a finite-state machine / grammar alongside generation to mask out illegal next tokens (`-∞`), guaranteeing **100% valid JSON or tool schemas**—but it NEVER guarantees the values inside are true! Separate **intrinsic hallucinations** (contradicting the supplied RAG passage) from **extrinsic hallucinations** (inventing unsupported facts beyond the context), and watch RL/DPO/GRPO for **reward hacking** (verbosity inflation, sycophancy or exploiting brittle graders).
detail: Feynman distinction: constrained decoding is like a web form dropdown that forces you to type a valid 5-digit ZIP code—it stops parser crashes, not wrong addresses! Even subtlety matters: forcing JSON keys in an unnatural order (putting `"verdict": true` *before* `"reasoning"`) can actually *hurt* accuracy because causal tokens can't revise an early boolean! Meanwhile, Goodhart's Law hits post-training hard: if human raters or LLM judges slightly prefer longer, confident-sounding bullet lists, DPO/RL policies quickly bloat answer length by 2×; in code/agent RL (GRPO), an un-sandboxed policy may delete a failing test or hardcode expected cases unless tests are hidden/read-only.
example: Schema-constrained JSON `{ "q3_revenue_millions": 999.9, "citation": "doc_1" }` parses on try #1 with zero retries, yet `999.9` can still be fabricated—you still need deterministic span/math verification.
follow: Why should structured schemas place a short `'evidence_quote'` or `'step_by_step_check'` field *before* `'final_decision'` in autoregressive JSON output?

q: ARMA, ARIMA and stationarity?
a: ARMA typically models a stationary series; ARIMA incorporates differencing to address nonstationarity. The ADF test has a unit-root null: a small p-value is evidence against that null, not a generic proof of every kind of stationarity. Evaluate with time-ordered backtests and account for seasonality.
follow: Why can ordinary shuffled cross-validation mislead?
detail: Most ML models assume rows are interchangeable—time series violates that through trend, seasonality and autocorrelation! A raw stock price or cumulative user curve drifts upward so its mean and variance change every month (non-stationary). Differencing (`y_t − y_{t-1}`, the `'I'` in ARIMA) turns levels into changes so past relationships stay meaningful, and evaluation must use **rolling/expanding origin backtests** rather than random K-fold splits.
example: Predicting tomorrow's temperature with random train/test split lets Tuesday and Thursday leak Wednesday's exact cold front into training!

q: Softmax, sparse and linear attention: what changes?
a: Dense softmax attention compares each query with every allowed key. Sparse or sliding-window attention restricts which token pairs interact. Recurrent linear attention summarizes earlier keys/values in a fixed-size state for fixed head dimensions, changing the representation of history.

rows: FlashAttention
Memory traffic and materialized score storage.
Computes dense softmax attention; quadratic pairwise work remains.
Sliding-window attention
Only a bounded neighborhood is scored per layer.
Distant access needs propagation, global tokens or other mechanisms.
Recurrent linear attention
No growing token-by-token cache in those layers.
Compresses history; it is not identical to softmax and may lose fine-grained recall.

nuance: “Linear” is scaling in sequence length with width held fixed, not a linear function of the input. Parallel chunk algorithms can train recurrent-style layers efficiently; a mathematical recurrence need not imply a fully sequential training kernel.
detail: Why can't pure linear/RNN compression completely replace softmax attention everywhere? Think of copying a random 12-digit confirmation code buried 40,000 tokens back: dense softmax keeps an uncompressed slot per past token in the KV cache (`exact lookup`), whereas recurrent linear attention squashes all 40,000 tokens into one fixed-size matrix `S_t` (`lossy summary`). Modern long-context hybrids interleave mostly fast linear/sliding layers with periodic full-attention layers to get both speed and exact needle-in-a-haystack recall.
example: In a 3:1 hybrid of 32 layers, 24 linear layers hold constant-size state `O(d²)` while only 8 full-attention layers grow a KV cache—cutting KV memory ~4×.
follow: Which task breaks first when you compress KV history into a fixed-size state: broad summarization or exact passkey/UUID retrieval?

q: What is Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)?
a: KDA is a gated recurrent linear-attention mechanism. Its memory stores key–value associations; a delta-rule update writes a correction to the value currently predicted for a key. KDA adds feature-wise forgetting, finer-grained than a single scalar decay per head.
notation: Use column vectors and S of shape \((d_v,d_k)\). \(\beta_t\) controls the write. This is the ungated intuition, not the full KDA equation.
nuance: Kimi Linear (2025) interleaves three KDA layers with one full-attention MLA layer. KDA layers keep fixed-size state, but the hybrid still has growing caches in its full-attention layers. Compressed memory trades exact historical access for efficiency; this is an architecture change, unlike FlashAttention’s exact-attention kernel optimization.
detail: Plain linear attention just keeps adding `v_t k_tᵀ` into memory matrix `S_t`, which eventually overflows like writing new phone numbers on top of old ones without an eraser! The **delta rule** turns `S_t` into an associative key–value dictionary: before writing `(k_t, v_t)`, it checks what `S_{t-1} k_t` currently recalls and writes only the *error correction* `(v_t − S_{t-1} k_t) k_tᵀ`, while KDA's per-channel gates selectively erase stale dimensions.
example: If `x = 5` at token 10 and `x = 9` at token 200, un-gated additive linear attention blurs both values together; a gated delta update overwrites key `'x'` toward `9`.
follow: Why does Kimi Linear still keep 1 full-attention layer for every 3 KDA layers instead of going 100% KDA?
